objective: By the end of this lesson you can read your airplane's performance charts, explain what changes performance, compute weight and balance, fix an out-of-limits load, and say why the real airplane may do worse than the chart.
why: The POH numbers tell you if this runway, this load and today's air will work. Most pilot-caused accidents happen on takeoff and landing, where these numbers matter most [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

prereading.what: Density altitude, takeoff/landing factors, and the sample chart problems (Sample Problems 1-3).
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 11, 11-1 to 11-28

prereading.what: Weight and balance terms, the computational method (Figure 10-5), and shifting/adding/removing weight.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 10, 10-1 to 10-11

prereading.what: Effect of weight and CG location on structure, stability and stall speed.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 5, 5-42 to 5-44

warmup: Same airplane, same runway. Why might it lift off easily on a cold January morning but use most of the runway on a hot August afternoon?

key_terms.def: Altitude shown when the altimeter is set to 29.92 "Hg. Basis for performance charts.
Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. The airplane performs as if it were at this altitude.
Finding a value between two printed chart values.
Imaginary line, set by the maker, that all arms are measured from.
Distance in inches from the datum to an item. Plus (+) if aft, minus (-) if forward.
Total moment / total weight. The point where the airplane would balance.
The forward and aft CG points (by weight) the CG must stay inside for flight.
Pilot, passengers, baggage, usable fuel and drainable oil. Max gross weight minus basic empty weight.
Distance on the runway, and distance to clear a 50-foot obstacle.

body.p: The performance section of the AFM/POH gives takeoff, climb, range, endurance, descent and landing data. Using it is mandatory for safe operation [[1:257|PHAK 11-1]].

The data is not standardized. Some makers use tables, some use graphs. Some base charts on standard conditions, some on pressure altitude, some on density altitude. Know which one your chart uses [[1:258|PHAK 11-2]].

bullets: Charts come from test flights in a new airplane, flown with average piloting skill, with airplane and engine in good working order [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].
Every chart lists its conditions and notes. Read them first [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].
Before every flight, compute performance. Every flight is different [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.103(b): before any flight the PIC must know runway lengths at airports of intended use, and the takeoff and landing distance data [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]]. 14 CFR 91.9(a): you must comply with the operating limitations in the AFM, markings and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9]].

check.q: Your POH chart was built from a new airplane flown by an average pilot. What does that mean for your old club airplane?
check.a: Your numbers may be worse. Adjust if the airplane is not in good working order or skill is below average [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].

chunks.title: Air density: pressure and density altitude

body.p: Standard atmosphere at sea level: 15 °C (59 °F) and 29.92 "Hg (1013.2 mb). Standard temperature drops about 2 °C (3.5 °F) per 1,000 feet; pressure drops about 1 "Hg per 1,000 feet [[1:258|PHAK 11-2]].
Thin air reduces three things [[1:258|PHAK 11-2]]:

bullets: Power: the engine takes in less air.
Thrust: the propeller is less efficient.
Lift: thin air exerts less force on the wings.

body.p: Pressure altitude: set 29.92 and read the altimeter, or correct field elevation for the altimeter setting, or use a flight computer [[1:259|PHAK 11-3]]. Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. The airplane performs as if it were at the density altitude [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]].
Source: [[1:260|PHAK 11-4]]. Humidity has no chart or rule of thumb, but moist air is less dense. Expect less performance when humid [[1:261|PHAK 11-5]].

callout.text: "High, hot and humid" = high density altitude = poor performance.

body.p: Worked example, PHAK Sample Problem 1 [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]]: field elevation 5,883 ft, OAT 70 °F, altimeter 30.10.

bullets: Step 1: In the table, 30.10 gives a correction of -165. Pressure altitude = 5,883 - 165 = 5,718 ft.
Step 2: Go up from 70 °F to the 5,718-ft pressure altitude line (about two-thirds of the way from 5,000 to 6,000).
Step 3: Go straight left. Density altitude is about 7,700 ft.

body.p: Why it matters: at 5,000 ft pressure altitude a ground run of 790 ft on a standard day may be closer to 1,000 ft when it is 20 °C above standard [[1:260|PHAK 11-4]].

check.q: Field 5,883 ft, altimeter 30.10, OAT 70 °F. Pressure altitude? Density altitude?
check.a: 5,718 ft pressure altitude; about 7,700 ft density altitude [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]].

body.p: Charts usually assume a paved, level, smooth, dry runway [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Real runways differ.

head: Condition
Effect
rows: Grass, gravel, soft, mud, snow, standing water
Less braking; hydroplaning can remove braking and steering [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]

body.p: Runway surface and slope are listed in the Chart Supplement [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

callout.text: Minimum hydroplaning speed = 9 x square root of main tire pressure (psi). 36 psi: 9 x 6 = 54 knots. Once it starts, hydroplaning can continue well below that speed [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

check.q: Wind affects landing distance the same way it affects takeoff. A tailwind equal to 10% of your landing speed adds about how much?

body.p: Weight: a 10% heavier takeoff weight gives about 5% higher takeoff speed, at least 9% slower acceleration, and at least 21% longer takeoff distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. On landing, 10% more weight gives about 10% more landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
Overloading also means higher stall speed, reduced climb, lower ceiling, slower cruise, and a longer landing roll [[1:246|PHAK 10-2]].

Configuration: flaps give more lift (lower approach and landing speed) and more drag (steeper descent), and shorten the landing roll [[24:172|AFH 9-1]]. Up to 15° of flap gives mostly lift; more than 15° adds a lot of drag [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. Gear down and flaps down reduce excess thrust and power, so climb gets worse [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].
Pilot technique:

bullets: 10% extra speed at takeoff = about 21% more takeoff distance [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].
10% extra speed at landing = at least 21% more landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
Lifting off too slow: ground effect hides the extra drag. Climbing out of ground effect too slow can leave you unable to climb, worst at high weight and high density altitude [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].
A 5-knot error from VX or VY can cut climb performance a lot in some airplanes [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Lean the mixture per the POH. Example chart note: above 3,000 ft, lean for max rpm at full throttle before takeoff [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

callout.text: The most critical takeoffs combine high gross weight, high altitude, high temperature and unfavorable wind [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

check.q: You fly final 10% fast. About how much longer is your landing distance?

body.p: Combined graph, PHAK Sample Problem 2 [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]]: pressure altitude 2,000 ft, OAT 22 °C, weight 2,600 lb, headwind 6 knots, 50-ft obstacle.

bullets: 1. Up from 22 °C to the 2,000-ft line. Across to the first reference line.
2. Follow the diagonals to 2,600 lb. Across to the second reference line.
3. Follow the diagonals to 6 knots headwind. Across to the third reference line.
4. Straight across = ground roll 700 ft. Follow diagonals to 50 ft = total 1,400 ft.
5. Speed table: lift-off 63 knots, 68 knots at 50 ft [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]].

callout.text: The red line drawn on the PHAK's own graph ends near 800 / 1,450 ft, but its worked answer says 700 / 1,400 ft [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]]. Read charts carefully and round toward the safe side.

body.p: Table, PHAK Sample Problem 3 [[1:277|PHAK 11-21]]: 2,400 lb, pressure altitude 3,000 ft, 30 °C, 18-knot headwind.

bullets: Table reads: ground roll 1,325 ft; total over 50 ft 2,480 ft.
Note 2: decrease 10% for each 9 knots of headwind. 18 knots = 20% off.
Same for total: 1,984 ft over a 50-ft obstacle.

body.p: Interpolation: for 2,500 ft at 20 °C in this table, average the 2,000-ft and 3,000-ft ground rolls: (1,115 + 1,230) / 2 = 1,173 ft [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]].

callout.text: When in doubt, round toward the worse condition. It gives a small safety margin [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]]. On combined graphs a small error early becomes a big error at the end [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].

check.q: Why apply the headwind correction after reading the table, not before?
check.a: The table is built for zero wind (see Conditions). The notes then tell you how to correct: 10% less per 9 knots headwind [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

chunks.title: Climb, cruise, crosswind, landing and stall charts

body.p: Same method on every chart: read conditions, enter the chart, apply notes. The PHAK's own sample answers:

head: Chart
Given
Answer
rows: Subtract departure from cruise values (6.0 - 3.5 gal, 10.5 - 6 min, 15 - 9 NM): 2.5 gal, 4.5 min, 6 NM. The PHAK text rounds the time to 4 min [[1:279|PHAK 11-23]]
10 min, 21 lb, 20 NM, +10% for 7 °C above standard = 11 min, 23.1 lb (3.85 gal), 22 NM [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]]
Interpolate: 1,105 ft total, 457.5 ft ground roll [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]]
Power off, flaps and gear down, 45° bank

callout.text: Landing weight is not takeoff weight. Recompute it for the fuel you burned [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]].

check.q: The climb table gives 21 lb of fuel. How many gallons is that before the temperature correction?
check.a: 21 / 6 = 3.5 gal. Avgas weighs 6 lb per gallon [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]].

body.p: Moment = weight x arm. CG = total moment / total weight. Arms aft of the datum are plus; forward are minus [[1:250|PHAK 10-6]].

The pilot controls loading and fuel, the two things that change both weight and CG [[1:248|PHAK 10-4]]. In many airplanes you cannot fill all seats, baggage and tanks and still be within limits [[1:248|PHAK 10-4]].

bullets: Standard weights: gasoline 6 lb/gal, oil 7.5 lb/gal [[1:249|PHAK 10-5]]. Use actual weights when you have them.
Fuel in the wings near the CG: burning it moves the CG little in most small airplanes [[1:255|PHAK 10-11]].
Baggage areas have their own limits. A compartment may be placarded for 20 lb because of floor strength [[1:139|PHAK 5-42]].

head: CG too far forward
CG too far aft
rows: Hard to raise the nose; may be unable to flare [[1:247|PHAK 10-3]]
Less stable; hard stall and spin recovery [[1:247|PHAK 10-3]]
Very light control forces; easy to overstress [[1:247|PHAK 10-3]]
Can enter a flat spin you cannot recover from [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]]

body.p: Computational method, PHAK Figure 10-5: 3,320 lb total, 281,430 in-lb total moment. 281,430 / 3,320 = 84.8 in. Limits are 78-86 in, so it is loaded within limits [[1:251|PHAK 10-7]].

check.q: A 50-lb bag at station 100. What is its moment?

chunks.title: Worked weight and balance: takeoff and landing

body.p: From the Weight & Balance Handbook single-engine example [[22:50|W&B 5-2]]. Limits: max 3,100 lb takeoff, 2,950 lb landing. CG range +40.9 to +46.0 at 3,100 lb; +33.0 to +46.0 at 2,250 lb or less.
Numbers from [[22:51|W&B Figure 5-3]]. CG = 131,806.2 / 3,027 = 43.54 in aft of datum [[22:50|W&B 5-2]].
Plot 3,027 lb and 43.54 in on the CG limits chart. The point is inside the envelope for takeoff, but the airplane is 77 lb over the 2,950-lb landing weight [[22:50|W&B 5-2]].
All phases of flight: to land right after takeoff, it must first burn 77 lb of fuel (slightly less than 13 gallons) [[22:54|W&B 5-6]].

callout.text: Check the landing CG too. Our math with the handbook numbers: burning 77 lb of fuel at the fuel arm of 46.6 removes 3,588.2 lb-in. 131,806.2 - 3,588.2 = 128,218.0 lb-in. 128,218.0 / 2,950 = 43.46 in. At 2,950 lb the limits are about +39.5 (forward) to +46.0 (aft), so it is still inside the envelope on Figure 5-5.
Weight x Arm = Moment. Add weights, add moments, divide. Then check the envelope at takeoff AND at landing.

check.q: Is this airplane legal to take off? To land right away?
check.a: Takeoff: yes, inside the envelope. Landing right away: no, 77 lb over the 2,950-lb max landing weight [[22:50|W&B 5-2]].

body.p: If the CG is out of limits, move people or baggage. Too far forward: move weight aft. Too far aft: move weight forward [[22:17|W&B 1-3]]. Shifting weight keeps total weight the same but changes the total moment [[1:254|PHAK 10-10]].
Shift formula: weight shifted / total weight = change in CG / distance shifted [[1:255|PHAK 10-11]].
Worked example [[1:255|PHAK 10-11]]: 7,800 lb, CG 81.5 in, aft limit 80.5 in. How much cargo must move from station 150 to station 30?

bullets: CG must move 1.0 in. Weight is moved 120 in.
Weight to shift / 7,800 = 1.0 / 120.
Weight to shift = 65 lb.

body.p: Adding or removing weight [[1:255|PHAK 10-11]]: weight added (or removed) / new total weight = change in CG / distance between the weight and the old CG.

bullets: Add 140 lb at station 150 to 6,860 lb at CG 80.0: 140/7,000 = CG change/70, so CG moves 1.4 in aft. New CG 81.4 in.
Remove 100 lb at station 150 from 6,100 lb at CG 80.0: 100/6,000 = CG change/70, so CG moves 1.2 in forward. New CG 78.8 in.

callout.text: Think first: which way should the CG move? Aft = add the change; forward = subtract it [[1:255|PHAK 10-11]].

check.q: 100 lb moves from station 30 to station 150. How much does the total moment change?

body.p: In steady flight, all upward forces balance all downward forces, and all forward forces balance all rearward forces. In level flight that is roughly lift = weight and thrust = drag [[1:99|PHAK 5-2]]. Lift depends on air density, speed, wing area and lift coefficient. Lift varies with the square of speed: double the speed, four times the lift [[1:101|PHAK 5-4]]. Lift and drag also vary directly with air density. In thinner air the airplane must fly a higher true airspeed at the same AOA [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]].

The wing always stalls at the same critical angle of attack. More weight needs more lift, and near the critical AOA the only way to get it is more speed [[1:101|PHAK 5-4]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor. 60° bank in a level turn = 2 Gs [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

CG and the tail: the CG is usually ahead of the center of lift, and this gives a nose-down tendency [[1:250|PHAK 10-6]]. Modern airplanes are designed to need a down load on the tail [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]. A forward CG needs more tail down-load. That adds to the load on the wing, so AOA, drag and stall speed go up [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]].

bullets: Forward CG: higher stall speed, higher control forces [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].
Aft CG: faster cruise (less drag) but less stable [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].
High density altitude: same indicated airspeed for takeoff and landing, but higher true airspeed, so longer runs [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

body.p: Climb needs excess power or thrust. More weight, more altitude, gear down or flaps down all reduce it [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. Below the speed for minimum power (region of reversed command), slower flight needs more power to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].

callout.text: Ground effect: within about one wingspan of the ground. Less induced drag. It can let you lift off too slow [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

check.q: Why does a forward CG raise stall speed?
check.a: The tail needs more down-load, which adds to the wing loading, so the stalling AOA is reached at a higher speed [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

chunks.title: Limitations and the gap between chart and reality

body.p: Airplane limitations you must respect:

head: Limit
What it protects
rows: Structure. Normal category is built for 3.8 G; a 100-lb overload adds a potential 380-lb structural overload [[1:139|PHAK 5-42]]
Never exceed. Structural damage or failure may result [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]
Max speed where limit load from gusts or full control deflection causes no structural damage [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]. Not protection against multiple full inputs [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]
Max speed with flaps extended. Air loads on flaps [[1:274|PHAK 11-18]]
Tested at up to 0.2 VS0; published in the AFM/POH [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]]

body.p: Why actual performance may be worse than the chart:

bullets: Test airplane was new and flown by an average pilot [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].
Engine or airplane not in good working order [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].
Humidity is not on the chart but still hurts [[1:261|PHAK 11-5]].
Runway not paved, level, smooth and dry [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Your technique: extra speed, early lift-off, late touchdown [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].
Max allowable weight may be more than a safe operating weight for high density altitude, wet grass or a short runway [[22:17|W&B 1-3]].

callout.text: Build a margin. The RMH sample personal minimums include shortest runway, highest terrain and highest density altitude [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]. For an unfamiliar airport, it suggests adding at least 500 ft to your runway minimum [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

check.q: Name three reasons the airplane may need more runway than the POH says.
check.a: Older airplane/engine, below-average technique (e.g. excess speed), and conditions not on the chart such as humidity or a grass or wet runway [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].

scenario.title: Hot afternoon, full airplane, short runway
scenario.setup: You plan a summer trip with two friends and bags. The departure airport sits at 5,883 ft, it is 70 °F, the altimeter is 30.10, and it is humid. The runway is grass. Your friends want to leave now and the tanks are full. The flight school's POH chart for a paved, dry runway shows you have enough runway, with a little left over.

questions.q: What density altitude will the airplane feel, and what does that do to performance?
questions.a: About 7,700 ft [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]]. Less power, less thrust and less lift, so longer takeoff and weaker climb [[1:258|PHAK 11-2]]. Humidity makes it worse [[1:261|PHAK 11-5]].

questions.q: The chart assumes paved, level and dry. What must you add for grass?
questions.a: Apply the chart's grass note. Example: one PHAK table adds 15% of the ground roll for dry grass [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. Any surface that is not hard and smooth lengthens the ground roll [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

questions.q: With full tanks and three people, what limit might you break, and how do you fix it?
questions.a: Max weight or CG limits. Many airplanes cannot fill all seats, baggage and tanks and stay in limits; reduce fuel or baggage [[1:248|PHAK 10-4]]. The max weight may also be too high for high density altitude or a soft field [[22:17|W&B 1-3]].

questions.q: Your friends say 'the chart says it works.' Why is that not enough?
questions.a: The chart came from a new airplane flown by an average pilot. Adjust for an older airplane or below-average technique [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. Lifting off too slow can leave you stuck in ground effect at high weight and density altitude [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].
Recompute with honest numbers, lighten the load, consider leaving in the cool morning, and keep a margin set by personal minimums made before the day of the flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

skills.do: Compute weight and CG for the planned load from the POH, check it on the envelope for takeoff and for landing (after fuel burn), and show how you would fix an out-of-limits CG by moving or removing weight.
skills.practice: Work the W&B Handbook example (3,027 lb, 43.54 in) by hand, then do your own airplane with you, a passenger, full fuel and bags. Then move a bag forward/aft and recompute with the shift formula [[1:255|PHAK 10-11]].

skills.do: Use your airplane's POH charts to find takeoff and landing distance, climb, cruise and crosswind values for given conditions, including notes and interpolation, and compare them to the runway.
skills.practice: Redo PHAK Sample Problems 1-3, then use your POH for today's weather at your home airport and one high or short airport [[1:276|PHAK 11-20]].

options: Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature
Indicated altitude with the local altimeter setting
quiz.why: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature [[1:259|PHAK 11-3]].

quiz.q: Which combination gives the highest density altitude?
options: High elevation, cold, and dry air
Low elevation, hot, and dry air
quiz.why: High elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity raise density altitude [[1:260|PHAK 11-4]].

quiz.q: A table gives 1,325 ft ground roll for zero wind. The note says decrease 10% per 9 knots of headwind. With 18 knots of headwind, ground roll is:
Ground roll is 1,115 ft at 2,000 ft and 1,230 ft at 3,000 ft. At 2,500 ft it is about:
Total weight 3,320 lb, total moment 281,430 lb-in, CG limits 78-86 in. The CG is:
The W&B Handbook example weighs 3,027 lb with a 2,950-lb max landing weight. What must happen before landing?
options: Nothing, it is in the envelope
quiz.why: It is 77 lb over landing weight and must burn 77 lb (slightly less than 13 gal) first [[22:54|W&B 5-6]].

quiz.q: An airplane weighs 7,800 lb with CG 81.5 in; aft limit 80.5 in. How much cargo must move from station 150 to station 30?
Compared to an aft CG, a forward CG gives:
options: Lower stall speed and faster cruise
Higher stall speed and higher control forces
quiz.why: Forward CG: higher stall speed and higher elevator forces [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

quiz.q: A tailwind that is 10% of takeoff speed changes takeoff distance by about:
Why might real takeoff distance be longer than the POH value?
options: Charts are from a new airplane flown by an average pilot in good working order
quiz.why: Charts come from new airplanes, average skill, good working order [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].

takeaways: Read every chart's conditions and notes first, then apply corrections [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]].
High, hot, humid and heavy all mean longer runs and weaker climbs [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].
Weight x arm = moment; total moment / total weight = CG. Check the envelope at takeoff and at landing.
Out of CG limits? Move weight toward the side the CG needs to go, or remove weight [[22:17|W&B 1-3]].
Extra speed costs runway: 10% fast = about 21% more distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].
The chart is a best case. Add a margin.
cfi_notes: Have the student say each chart's conditions out loud before entering it. Missing 'zero wind' or 'paved, dry' is the most common error.
Students often apply headwind credit twice or forget the tailwind penalty. Use PHAK Sample Problem 3 to show the note math.
Make them compute landing weight and landing CG, not just takeoff. The W&B Handbook example (3,027 lb, 77 lb over landing weight) is a good trap.
Examiners often ask the student to fix an aft-CG load: move a bag forward or reduce rear weight, then recompute.
Ask 'what would make actual performance worse than this number?' Expect technique, airplane condition, humidity, surface, slope.
In PHAK Figure 11-24 the 2,000-lb, 30 °C column has some out-of-order values (e.g. 2,145 at 5,000 ft). Point out that charts can contain errors and must be read carefully.
Fly it: show the student real ground roll and climb on a hot day vs. the chart, and the effect of 10 knots extra on final.
PHAK Figure 11-23's drawn trace reads about 800 / 1,450 ft while its text answer is 700 / 1,400 ft. Use it to show why careful chart reading matters.
gaps: Actual V-speeds, weights, CG limits, flap settings and chart values for the student's airplane must come from that airplane's POH/AFM and current weight and balance record; the handbooks only give generic samples.
No handbook rule of thumb exists for the humidity correction; the PHAK only says to expect lower performance [[1:261|PHAK 11-5]].
Lateral (side-to-side) CG is mentioned but not computed for most airplanes in these sources.

activities.title: Find the CG: put the steps in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: List each weight: airplane, people, fuel and bags
Multiply each weight by its arm to get its moment
Add up the total weight and the total moment
Divide total moment by total weight to find the CG
Check weight and CG on the envelope for takeoff
Take out the fuel you will burn and check again for landing

activities.title: True or false: balance and aerodynamics

cards.s: Moving a heavy bag from the rear baggage area to a front seat moves the CG forward.
cards.why: Yes. Moving weight forward lowers the total moment, so the CG moves forward [[1:254|PHAK 10-10]].

cards.s: Moving a bag from one spot to another inside the airplane changes the total weight.
cards.why: No. Total weight stays the same. Only the total moment, and so the CG, changes [[1:254|PHAK 10-10]].

cards.s: In most small airplanes, burning fuel from the wing tanks moves the CG a lot.
cards.why: No. The tanks sit near the CG, so burning fuel changes it very little [[1:255|PHAK 10-11]].

cards.s: With an aft CG, the airplane cruises a little faster but is less stable.
cards.why: Yes. The tail needs less down-load, so drag is lower. But stability goes down as the CG moves aft [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]].

cards.s: At a high-altitude airport, you should lift off at a higher indicated airspeed than at sea level.
cards.why: No. Use the same indicated airspeed. Your true airspeed is higher, which is why the run is longer [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

cards.s: A level 60° bank turn puts 2 Gs on the airplane, so it stalls at a higher speed.
cards.why: Yes. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, and a 60° level turn is 2 Gs [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a short local flight that stays in the traffic pattern. Under 14 CFR 91.103, what must you still know before you go?
options: Runway lengths and the airplane's takeoff and landing distance data
Alternatives if the flight cannot be completed
Weather reports and forecasts for a route
final_quiz.why: For any flight, the PIC must know runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data. Weather, fuel, alternatives and delays are listed for IFR flights or flights not near an airport [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

final_quiz.q: Field elevation is 1,200 ft and the altimeter setting is 29.60. Using the altimeter correction table, what is the pressure altitude?
final_quiz.why: 29.60 is below 29.92, so the table says add 298 ft. 1,200 + 298 = 1,498 ft [[1:259|PHAK 11-3]].

final_quiz.q: A runway slopes uphill toward the east. There is no wind. Compared to a level runway, what should you expect on a takeoff to the east?
options: No change, because slope only affects landings
A shorter run, but a longer climb
final_quiz.why: An upslope slows acceleration, so the takeoff ground run is longer. Landing uphill usually shortens the landing roll [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your main tires are inflated to 49 psi. About what speed can dynamic hydroplaning begin on a wet runway?
final_quiz.why: Multiply the square root of tire pressure by 9: 9 x 7 = 63 knots. Once it starts, hydroplaning can continue well below that speed [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

final_quiz.q: On a short runway, a pilot holds the airplane on the ground until 10% above the POH lift-off speed "for safety." About how much more takeoff distance does that use?
options: None, extra speed only improves the climb
final_quiz.why: Takeoff distance varies with the square of takeoff speed, so 10% extra speed adds about 21% [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

final_quiz.q: Use the short-field takeoff table: 2,400 lb, sea level, 20 °C, 4-knot tailwind. What ground roll should you plan?
final_quiz.why: The table gives 925 ft for zero wind. Note 2 adds 10% for each 2 knots of tailwind, so 4 knots = 20%. 925 + 185 = 1,110 ft [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]].

final_quiz.q: After loading, total weight is 2,400 lb and total moment is 103,200 lb-in. The CG limits are 35.0 to 47.3 in. Where is the CG?
final_quiz.why: CG = total moment / total weight: 103,200 / 2,400 = 43.0 in, which is between 35.0 and 47.3 [[1:251|PHAK 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: An airplane weighs 3,000 lb with its CG at 47.0 in. The aft limit is 46.0 in. You move a 90-lb bag from station 120 to station 70. What is the new CG?
final_quiz.why: Weight shifted / total weight = CG change / distance moved: 90 / 3,000 = CG change / 50, so the CG moves 1.5 in forward. 47.0 - 1.5 = 45.5 in, inside the limit [[1:255|PHAK 10-11]].

final_quiz.q: Max landing weight is 2,550 lb. You take off at 2,610 lb and then need to return and land. How much fuel must you burn first?
final_quiz.why: You are 60 lb over. Avgas weighs 6 lb per gallon, so 60 / 6 = 10 gallons [[1:249|PHAK 10-5]]. An airplane can be legal for takeoff but too heavy to land right away [[22:54|W&B 5-6]].

final_quiz.q: In the W&B Handbook sample airplane, you want to put 80 lb of bags in baggage area B. Total weight and CG would still be in limits. Can you?
options: Yes, total weight and CG are all that matter
No, area B is limited to 50 lb
Yes, as long as area A is empty
No, area B is limited to 60 lb
final_quiz.why: Area B is limited to 60 lb and area A to 100 lb [[22:50|W&B 5-2]]. A compartment limit protects the floor structure even when weight and CG are fine [[1:139|PHAK 5-42]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane's VS0 is 50 knots. In certification testing, it had to be shown able to land in a 90° crosswind of at least:
final_quiz.why: Airplanes are tested in 90° crosswinds up to 0.2 VS0: 0.2 x 50 = 10 knots. The max demonstrated crosswind is in the AFM/POH [[1:281|PHAK 11-25]].

final_quiz.q: On a hot day at max weight, why is it dangerous to lift off below the recommended speed?
options: Ground effect adds drag, so the airplane cannot accelerate
Stall speed is lower near the ground, so it may stall higher up
Ground effect hides the extra drag, and the airplane may not climb out of it
The airspeed indicator reads high in ground effect
final_quiz.why: Ground effect reduces induced drag, so the airplane may seem able to fly too slow. At high density altitude, high temperature or max weight it may lift off but be unable to climb out of ground effect [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your personal minimum for runway length is 2,500 ft. You plan a trip to an airport you have never visited. The RMH suggests raising that minimum to at least:
final_quiz.why: For unfamiliar airports, the RMH suggests adding at least 500 ft to your runway length minimum: 2,500 + 500 = 3,000 ft [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
